stage1/problem/A1/v1:
Problem: Can MVFA's segmentation adapters — which today learn localisation only from pixel masks of BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC — learn transferable localisation from image-level labels alone? We replace the Dice and Focal seg_loss with a multiple-instance objective on the segmentation-branch patch-to-text similarity map at each of the four levels (primary operator: mean of the top 2% of patch anomaly probabilities; max and mean pooling as ablations) and train on all five source datasets with masks discarded. Hypothesis: because each patch is scored against a shared text anchor, image-level supervision forces patch-level anomaly evidence to align with the text 'abnormal' direction, so localisation learned this way transfers to the unseen modality and retains at least 80% of the mask-supervised pixel-level AUROC. Outcomes on the held-out modality: pixel-level AUROC and PRO, image-level AUROC, the per-level localisation quality (which levels produce useful maps), and a label-budget curve comparing image-labelled training on all datasets with mask-supervised training on 10-100% of the masked images.

Rationale: Reviewers rated relevance and feasibility highest and asked for an explicit, distinctive hypothesis, the value of k, the level at which the loss applies, and a decision-relevant label-budget view. The hypothesis now states what is specific to the vision-language setting: localisation through text-anchored patch similarities rather than class-activation maps, tested across modalities. The operator is fixed (top 2%) and applied at all four levels with a per-level analysis. The label-budget curve answers the practical question a site faces — whether many cheaply labelled images can substitute for few masked ones. The change remains a single loss term in the public training script, evaluated under the shared protocol with source-validation model selection.
stage1/problem/A2/v1:
Problem: Is agreement across MVFA's four feature levels a reliable confidence signal for source-free adaptation to a new modality? Starting from source-trained MVFA, we pseudo-label pixels of an unlabelled target pool only where all four levels' zero-shot maps agree (lowest or highest 10% at every level), fine-tune both segmentation and detection adapters for three self-training rounds with losses restricted to those pixels, and compare against single-level (deepest-layer) confidence with the same pixel budget. Outcomes on a disjoint 50/50 test split: image AUROC, pixel AUROC and PRO versus unlabelled pool size N; the precision of the pseudo-labels against ground-truth masks; and the N at which performance matches few-shot MVFA with K = 4 labelled normal and abnormal images.

Rationale: Reviewers asked why cross-level agreement should be better than single-level confidence, for the self-training schedule, and for failure analysis. The problem is now centred on that comparison, measures pseudo-label precision directly, and fixes three rounds with both adapter sets updated. The deployment decision (how many unlabelled scans replace K labelled pairs) remains the practical outcome.
stage1/problem/B1/v1:
Problem: Can MVFA's few-shot fusion be made inductive — scoring each image on its own, without the test-set min-max normalisation in the released code — without losing AUROC, and does this give a threshold that transfers to unseen modalities? The inductive fusion standardises each branch using leave-one-out statistics of the K normal support images (each support's zero-shot map, and its few-shot map against a memory bank built from the other K-1 supports, pooled over patches and levels), adds the standardised branches, and pools the fused map with the mean of its top 2% pixels; the threshold is the 95th percentile of the supports' leave-one-out image scores. Primary outcome: image- and pixel-level AUROC of inductive versus transductive fusion on every held-out modality and K in {2, 4, 8, 16}. Motivating measurement: the spread of the transductive AUROC across random test subsets and at 10% and 50% prevalence. Secondary outcomes: sensitivity at the support-derived threshold, realised specificity, F1 and expected calibration error.

Rationale: Reviewers asked to single out the primary question and to define the leave-one-out statistics exactly. The primary question is now whether per-image (deployable) scoring matches the published transductive scoring; the test-set dependence analysis motivates it, and thresholded metrics are secondary. The leave-one-out procedure is fully specified, including pooling across levels to keep K = 2 well-defined. The change is confined to test_few.py, needs no training beyond re-running the baseline under the shared protocol, and directly addresses the verified limitations G8, G9, G11 and G17.
stage1/problem/B2/v1:
Problem: In zero-shot deployment, does a false-positive guarantee calibrated on normal images of the source modalities hold on an unseen BMAD modality, and does label-free covariate-shift weighting repair it? Per-image scores are computed without test-set normalisation, with max, mean and top-2% aggregation. Split-conformal thresholds are calibrated on held-out normal source images at nominal false-positive rates of 1%, 5% and 10%. The weighted variant reweights calibration images by density ratios estimated from a domain classifier between source calibration features and the unlabelled target batch, an explicit transductive-in-features, label-free assumption. Outcomes per held-out modality: realised false-positive rate with bootstrap intervals, coverage violation, sensitivity at the threshold, and how violation size relates to the source-target feature distance.

Rationale: Reviewers asked to make the transductive assumption of the weighting explicit and to explain what is learned beyond applying known techniques. The new element is the relation between violation size and a measurable source-target distance, which turns the result into a predictor of when a zero-shot threshold can be trusted. Everything else stays inference-only and fine-grained.
stage1/problem/D1/v1:
Problem: Does tying a compact set of learnable normal prototypes to MVFA's normal text anchor improve zero-shot transfer? At each adapter level, M prototypes are initialised from the normal text embedding plus small noise and trained jointly with the adapters on the source modalities, with a compactness loss pulling normal patches to their nearest prototype and a margin (set to the 95th percentile of normal-patch distances on source validation data) keeping abnormal patches away; the anomaly map adds the prototype distance to the text-similarity map. Outcomes: zero-shot image AUROC, pixel AUROC and PRO on the held-out modality for M in {8, 32}, versus MVFA and versus untied (randomly initialised) prototypes.

Rationale: Reviewers asked what is specific to the vision-language setting, how prototypes are initialised, and to limit tuning. Anchoring prototypes to the normal text embedding is the vision-language-specific element, comparing tied and untied prototypes tests it directly, and the margin is fixed from source statistics to keep tuning small.
stage1/problem/D2/v1:
Problem: Is the text side of MVFA a bottleneck, and does conditioning the normal anchor on the support normals help most on the modalities furthest from the source pool? First, the variance of zero- and few-shot AUROC over 20 random subsets of 5, 10 and 20 of the 35 templates is measured. Then the static normal anchor is shifted by a light projector applied to the mean adapted feature of the K support normals, with abnormal anchors matched many-to-one, and compared with test-image conditioning of the same projector. Hypothesis: support conditioning helps more than test-image conditioning, and most on modalities with the largest source-target feature distance. Outcomes: few-shot image AUROC, pixel AUROC and PRO per held-out modality, and template-sensitivity variance.

Rationale: Reviewers asked for an explicit hypothesis and a direct comparison with test-image conditioning; both are now part of the problem.
